en: May the four forms never waver,
May the sea-like host be exhausted.
When we lived in Kokon,
We were the ones who led the people,
We came from Kokon,
We did not devour your people,
We had seen the designs of Moscow.
Whatever day befell us,
We saw the enemy’s wrath,
Unable to withstand the cold wind,
Sickness pierced us to the marrow,
There was no remedy for our staggering,
Taking the relic into our midst,
With no solution left, we panicked,
Unable to find a place to sustain life,
We fled without finding rest.
When we lived in Kokon,
We were Kyrgyz wearing quilted coats,
We were pure people who fielded cannon,
With great courage when facing the enemy,
We had been khans for forty years.
Like a river flowing from the core,
We were blood against the enemy,
Like water scattered abroad,
We were souls under oppression,
The matter returned to its beginning,
If this affair falls upon our brow,
We will bow our necks to death.
We were humiliated by the empire,
Fleeing from God, we became desperate,
We became full from so much migration,
We now come before you.
From another crown and throne,
Who has not shaken and burned?
While the empire held power,
Who has not lived under confinement?
This is the affair in which we broke our pledge,
Saying Padishah Jeljetpes would come,
In truth, you did not become Kokon.
The people of this city,
When that khan still stood at their head,
A blue-gray steed with a sweeping tail,
We had defeated many and grown strong,
Our horses raced upon the open steppe,
We used to range across the mountains,
When fortune stood over our heads,
Even youths would answer us with words.
We are warriors who guard the people,
We are of Kalmak blood and lineage,
Beaten by the wrathful one,
We are wretches who fled the khagan.
We are a people of trusted companions,
Against the dark enemy outside,
We came with our arms opened wide.
We are fighters with dun-colored manes,
Binding bullets into our wounds,
We are poor men who have been wounded.
Ebegei and Kogoi, the two lions,
Dragging their tails, raising an uproar,
We are coursers that win the prize,
Even untrained, when loosed we took the wolf,
We are dark gyrfalcons.
We are heroes equal to you,
Having encountered the khan’s wrath,
Driven about, unable to find a resting place,
We are diminished men whose people are gone.
We have gone about saying, “Receive us,”
If you choose to break and take our fortune,
We are among the honored ones.
Turning from the dark path toward the light,
Guarding the world by a hair’s breadth,
We have been struck down by the khan’s wrath,
Led astray by dark belief,
Wandering without finding a people,
We are heroes who fled the khagan,
Ebegei and Kogoi, the two giants,
If you send us from the host, we are capable,
We will bring back his tulpar.
We are twelve heroic champions,
Breaking a horde and taking a horde,
We will move like a dark-maned stallion,
The blessed Ala-Too will not be clouded,
If we do not wait, we shall die.
Without seeing humiliation, hardship, or quarrel,
We shall return and see it from our camp.
If you accept us, blessed one,
If the enemy is a ruined soul,
We will serve as wings for you.
When I lived in Kokon,
The black Chinese settled in splendor,
I was khan over the black people,
In Talas I was padishah over the people,
In Chüy I was their horde,
Among the Jalal people I was their realm.
Pearl and coral, precious stones,
I alone wore them outwardly.
Asking about affairs among the Chinese,
I was a son who knew them,
Riding the cloud and cloaked in frost,
I was one of the heroes who roamed.
A true Kyrgyz man among the four,
A turn lasting six months,
Since then the Kyrgyz have not taken it.
We are becoming men,
My people remain without lawful union,
Before the khan, the eye of the horde,
Among the horde’s maidens,
As in former times last year,
In the city of conquest,
My ancestors gave birth to me.
Whatever kind of khan my ancestor was,
He was one who led the people.
Thus he did not scatter them,
What kind of man went to the Chinese,
Name the four of you before you go.
Let us give it exactly so.
He addressed these words to Ebegei.
Coming together, the seven consulted among themselves,
His mother and father had died,
He was raised from the treasury,
Saying he would become master of the mares,
Entrusting him to the judge of horses,
No living soul could catch the ant,
A great man called Kündö,
Who served his khan,
Had him tended for ten days.
Beginning with silver ingots,
Zhelzhetpes, the wind-swift pacer,
Saying the orphan had become a fine racer,
They gave him the name Zhelzhetpes.
A Muslim who struck down the south,
A deep-rooted lion from the Kyrgyz.
Coming from the Chinese khagan,
For the man who showed no favor,
Biting his tongue when he would not obey,
Making so many heads rise,
Taking so many lives,
As though testing their strength,
Crying out sharply, he went back,
His neck submitted to the yoke,
His head drawn toward ruin,
Unable to find wind, he languished,
His head made blind before the throne,
Saying he had departed from Chyng Tengir,
Searching without finding, unable to find rest,
The hero, with eleven warrior companions,
Saying that the khagan would come.
We shall not suffer torment from the people,
Ebegei and Kogoi, the two elders,
Let us remain in possession of it.
When they heard this news,
Looking ahead before them,
A lone scout from one detachment,
It was Jeljetpes himself,
Wrapped in complete reed-colored gear,
The time of his arrival had come.
Ebegey and Köböy, the two companions,
When they heard this news,
Setting straight what had been said,
Raising alarm among the many Kyrgyz,
Saying God had granted them a lion-like hero,
Naming a horse for the tethering,
Quickly proclaiming it through every world,
Mounted on Kertulpar,
He who ruled across the moonlit world,
To that lion-like warrior,
With the mottled swift horse,
With the letter written by Ebegey,
Sending news from the khan,
What the son of Kuman had seen,
To all the populous Kyrgyz people.
Ebegey and Köböy, lion-like men,
Sent an alarming letter to the people,
They quickly delivered the urgent news,
The people rushed about in turmoil,
A fierce conflict arose,
Hardship became plain to see.
When they spoke and raised the alarm,
Toward hero Kenen’s plain,
Back toward the iron fortress,
The populous Kyrgyz set their thoughts,
When Jeljetpes encamped,
Such was the people’s prosperity.
There was no shelter from grief,
The countless Chinese remained,
Even hearing it three times, none could stand,
What a wrathful enemy he was.
With no figure seen and no tracks left,
The coursers were on the summer pasture,
The milking mares stood tethered,
After one day had passed,
The tethered horse neighed aloud,
The people lay at rest,
In their comfortable encampment,
The dear people hunted everything.
The warriors shot antelope,
They freely gave themselves to games.
Riding kulan and flying hunting birds,
Mighty Kenen lay at rest.
Sixteen youths, with none at the right hand,
Among those thousands, not one remained,
There was no guard at the lookout,
Such was this wretched world.
There was no pass where a lord stood bound,
No place had been firmly secured,
The people spread out across the steppe,
Watching each ravine and pass,
The people lay there in full, surging numbers,
A people carrying their common nation behind them,
Scattering jests, they spoke their words,
Forty men among the active souls,
The dear people pursued their pleasures,
The people camped according to the Quran,
Shouting, drinking spirits and eating rich food,
The people grew drunk amid abundance.
While the people lay freely at ease,
To brave Kenen, the lion,
To the lion seated on the golden throne,
News reached him and words reached him,
A dark disturbance swiftly reached him,
Ebegei and Kogoi were elders,
Chyng Tengir had set out from Beijing,
Across the hills and hollows of Ala-Too,
They wrote that his words had exceeded bounds.
Kenen, vast as the world,
They wrote it all down as a message,
The forty tribes stirred,
Kinsmen of an age gathered as an army,
Their struggle became abundant torment,
It was written that they would come trampling forward.
Scattering venom upon Beshay land,
Reducing the prosperous years to misery,
Raising turmoil across the world and land,
Their dread emerging like wolves,
Breaking apart those who were valued.
It was written that Baytan would come.
Destroying the whole world,
It was written that he would come trampling forward.
The wrath of the heroes,
It was written that Karman would come,
Without calling it strength or hardship,
Turning those caught into a host,
It was written that he would come devouring.
With wealth beyond measure,
The hapless one ignorant of affairs,
Exchanging news like fierce men,
It was written that he would come slaughtering.
Not leaving those caught alone,
That hardship would drain his people,
It was written that he would come wearing them down.
Making widows of those with myriads,
Making slaves of the settled households,
Turning those caught to blood,
Gnawing whoever he encountered,
It was written that he would come slaughtering.
With boundless courage,
